rv.q: McCann gives Bonnie the petite power, almost, of another Piaf.
This is far from a terrible show.
There’s so much talent here, but sadly it gets lost on the road.
If there is a palatable musical route into the Bonnie and Clyde story, then neither Winston, Wildhorn nor the rest of creative team have discovered it.

Quite how the creative trio of Ivan Menchell (book), Don Black (lyrics) and Frank Wildhorn (music) managed to take the sizzling story of those two infamous Texan lover/criminals and render it simultaneously devoid of romance and thrill is bewildering.
Ultimately ‘Bonnie & Clyde’ feels weirdly oblivious to the reasons why Parker and Barrow are still famous a century on.
It means the show zips by faster than a 1934. Ford Model 40 B Fordor Deluxe sedan – high-octane musical thrills served by a top-notch company.
This bigger, bolder, better production is worth a shot, and few will feel robbed after seeing it.
Despite the flaws, the show is a great night out and I'm pretty sure that the fans won't care if the production's hype is a little hollow.
This musical misses the spirit of recklessness, cruelty and abandonment of morals that Bonnie and Clyde are known for.
Nick Winston's Bonnie & Clyde suffers from telling too much, rather than showing its audience what happened, ruining any pace.
It has a pulse but not a heart.
Arthur Penn's 1969 film with Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway ushered in a new era of movie violence but this production steers clear of graphic depictions.

cn.t: Mixed reception for this Depression-era outlaw musical, with critics praising the leads' chemistry and some strong musical moments, but finding the show oddly insubstantial and unable to decide whether it's romance or cautionary tale.
